tools.title: Gable & Rake Wall Stud Calculator
tools.desc: Calculate sloped gable and rake wall stud centerline cuts, face-edge lengths and total plate deductions with a coordinate schedule.
tools.formula: Gross height(x) = left gross height + x × pitch/12; net CENTER cut = gross height − total vertical plate deduction; left/right edge cuts = center cut ± stud face width × pitch / 24.
tools.example: 144 in wall, 96 in start height, 6:12 gives end height 168 in before plates
tools.limit: Reference vertical centerline and two edge cuts, not structural/cutting certification. Total plate deduction is assumed vertical and applied once; wall run is between end centers, not outside faces. Confirm actual plate geometry.

guidance.heading: Measure from the left reference center
guidance.text: The wall run is the distance between the two end stud centers, not the outside-to-outside framed dimension. Enter the gross wall height at the left and the rise per 12 inches of horizontal run. The layout lists each stud center at the requested on-center interval and includes the far-end reference center.

guidance.heading: Center cut versus face-edge cut
guidance.text: A sloped top plate crosses the left and right faces of a stud at different elevations. The tool exports the vertical centerline cut and both edge-cut heights based on the entered face width; they should not be treated as interchangeable marks. Deduct the total vertical plate height only once.

guidance.heading: Choose the right wall calculator
guidance.text: This page describes a single sloped-top reference. Use Wall Stud Count & Layout for a uniform-height wall, or Wall Framing with Doors & Windows when actual rough openings, kings, jacks or cripple pieces must appear in the takeoff. Check each reference against the built wall before cutting.

tools.title: Wall Framing with Doors & Windows
tools.desc: Compare multiple lumber lengths for studs, headers and sills with cut layouts, quoted purchase costs, SVG diagrams and CSV exports.

inputs.label: Stud stock price per purchased stick (0 = quote needed)
Header stock price per purchased stick (0 = quote needed)
Sill stock price per purchased stick (0 = quote needed)
Stud Option A price per stick (0 = off)
Stud Option B price per stick (0 = off)
Header Option A price per stick (0 = off)
Header Option B price per stick (0 = off)
Sill Option A price per stick (0 = off)
Sill Option B price per stick (0 = off)

tools.formula: Full stud cut = wallHeight − bottomPlate − topPlate; Jack = openingSill + openingHeight − bottomPlate. Header begins at rough-opening top and spans between inside King faces, over both Jacks. Header depth is user-defined, not an engineered size. Window sill sits directly below the opening and lower cripples below that. Upper/lower cripples reuse eligible nominal OC centers fully inside the opening and are clipped to horizontal-member faces. Nominal first-fit decreasing groups cut pieces by Stud, Header or Sill stock type, packs full pieces without splices, charges kerf between consecutive cuts on a stick, and reports planned sticks/offcuts and separately rounded purchase allowance per stock group. It is an estimate, not proven minimum waste. The quote-based material estimate multiplies each material family's purchased sticks (including reserve) by the user-entered price per stick, with planned and reserve costs separated. Zero means price not supplied; no total purchase price is claimed until each used material family has a quote. When alternative per-stick prices are entered, each material family compares all feasible single-stock-length FFD layouts plus one greedy mixed-length plan. The estimated winner is the lowest purchase cost among those evaluated plans, including separately rounded reserve sticks per chosen length. For fully quoted families with at most sixteen pieces, a bounded exhaustive assignment search can prove the minimum modeled purchase cost when all states are visited. For larger layouts or if the 40,000-state limit is reached, the displayed result remains a heuristic estimate without an optimality guarantee. Canonical memoization merges equivalent cut-allocation states with identical next-piece index and per-offer used bar lengths, enabling exact search on up to 16 pieces when the entire compressed search completes within 40,000 distinct states.
tools.example: 120 in between end centers, 96 in gross wall, 16 in OC, 1.5 in studs, 1.5 in bottom plate, 3 in top plates, 32–68 in door opening top 80 in, 5.5 in header depth: six regular studs, four King/Jack, one 39 in header and two 7.5 in upper cripples; 13 listed pieces (plates not in cut list).
tools.limit: NONSTRUCTURAL reference-only geometry. Enter actual header depth; no span selection, header strength, load design, fastening, opening tolerances or code approval. Horizontal spans represent one piece each (not a prescribed number of built-up header layers). Top of rough opening means underside of header. Sill = 0 selects a door; nonzero is a window sill elevation. Verify material and field cuts. Stock cutting is a deterministic first-fit estimate, not a certified globally optimal nesting algorithm. Profiles are deliberately separate (Stud/Header/Sill); do not combine them without verifying cross sections. No splices, trimming loss, defective boards, or cost/pricing assumptions. Rounding of fractions is display-only: CSV retains numeric dimensions. Cost inputs are not market prices and contain no automatic currency exchange, tax, delivery, labor, permit or hardware charges. Currency selection labels the entered quotes only; changing denomination never converts values. A quoted total is a material-only subtotal based on the chosen stock family configuration, not a job estimate. Optional stock length offers A and B are disabled when their per-stick quote is zero. An unquoted default length is excluded from the quoted comparison; quotes are user-provided and cannot prove a market-wide cheapest plan. When no priced offer exists, the original single-length unquoted estimate is preserved. A chosen mixed-size plan records each source bar's own purchased length and price. Quote values support two decimals only. An exact-cost certificate is valid ONLY if the entire bounded state-compressed search completed for every used, fully quoted family. It covers the finite quoted offers, no-splice whole-piece cuts, saw kerf between cuts, and per-length reserve rounding; it does not certify an overall construction budget or universally cheapest real-world purchase. Sixteen pieces per material group and 40,000 distinct (memoized) search states are hard browser limits. A partial search is never marked optimal. Reused equivalent cutting states are tracked separately from distinct visited states. A layout with 16 or fewer pieces is not automatically proven; reaching the distinct-state limit with incomplete search remains NOT CERTIFIED.

guidance.heading: Specify the underside-of-header datum
guidance.text: Opening sill + opening height is the underside of the header; the selected header depth rises ABOVE that line, while each jack stud ends at it. A header spans between the inner King faces and rests over the Jacks. The program does not size the header for loading or determine built-up header ply counts.

guidance.heading: Window sills and two cripple zones
guidance.text: For a window, the sill board sits immediately below the entered sill elevation. Lower cripples fill from the top of the bottom plate to the underside of the sill; upper cripples fill from the top of the header to the underside of the top plates. Only fully fitting nominal on-center positions are used; a zone of zero height yields no cripple.

guidance.heading: Unified center, face and cut-list coordinates
guidance.text: The wall length is measured from one end-stud center to the other. Regular studs that intersect rough openings or King/Jack faces are removed. Each output row stores horizontal extent, elevation and cut length and is reused directly for the schematic SVG and CSV. The diagram is NOT a 1:1 construction cutting template.

guidance.heading: Three stock families and conservative purchase allowance
guidance.text: Choose real purchased lengths for Stud, Header and Sill material separately. The cutting plan fits member cut lengths into each category using first-fit decreasing, charging one entered saw kerf between consecutive cuts; it never joins short offcuts into a longer board. The optional percentage adds whole reserve sticks to each used family, not to each individual cut. Purchase lengths should account for any additional trimming or defects not modeled.

guidance.heading: Fractional-inch worksheet vs numeric CSV
guidance.text: For inches, the measurement table shows approximate 1/16 or 1/32 inch fractions beside the precise decimal cut length. Print/PDF includes the same fractions; downloadable CSV cut lists and stock plan retain precise numeric lengths in the selected unit. Always measure actual lumber and recheck saw kerf.

guidance.heading: Enter supplier quotes rather than simulated market prices
guidance.text: Set a per-stick price for each stock family that actually has cuts. Prices are entered in the currency selected on the page (USD by default). A price of zero means no quote, not free material. The worksheet will withhold a complete purchase total until all used groups are priced. Changing the currency dropdown changes the denomination label, not the numbers or exchange rates.

guidance.heading: Printable purchasing ticket and cost breakdown
guidance.text: The summary separates planned sticks, extra reserve sticks, their costs and the user-entered stock price by profile. The print ticket lists the actual buy quantity and source length for each used material group, including the 'quote needed' state; a numeric CSV export supports spreadsheet budgeting. Verify external costs such as tax, delivery, waste from defects, structural framing and fasteners separately.

guidance.heading: Compare 8, 10 and 12-foot supplier offers by stock family
guidance.text: The standard stock length and price remain the Base offer. Expand Alternative stock offers to enter Option A (defaults to 120 inches / 10 feet) and Option B (defaults to 144 inches / 12 feet), with separate supplier prices for Stud, Header and Sill. A zero alternative price disables that alternative. Unquoted offers are not treated as free or silently included in the price comparison.

guidance.heading: Heuristic mixed-length plan and purchase quantities
guidance.text: For every family, the calculator compares complete single-length FFD cutting estimates and one greedy mixed-length cutting estimate when two or more offers are quoted. Selection uses quoted purchase cost including reserve; ties prefer less offcut. See each candidate's cost, purchased sticks, and remaining stock in the comparison table. The chosen purchase checklist groups quantities by exact offered stock length; the method does not certify a globally optimal or engineering-approved plan. When the per-family exhaustive search finishes, the comparison includes a certified plan and a separate proof table. Certification is deliberately withheld for more than sixteen cuts, search budget exhaustion, or missing quotations.

guidance.heading: How to interpret the optimality certificate
guidance.text: The proof only concerns the selected offered stock lengths and quoted per-stick prices, whole cuts with the entered kerf, and purchase reserve rounded independently for each offered length. If every required material family is quoted and its ≤16-piece exhaustive search completes within 40,000 distinct states, the quoted material subtotal is certified minimal for this model. Otherwise the page explicitly says NOT CERTIFIED. Taxes, defects, stock availability, shipping, structural approvals and unquoted cheaper offers are outside the proof. This release memoizes equivalent stock arrangements and counts 40,000 distinct search states rather than all equivalent permutations, so some larger layouts can now earn a certificate without raising the browser search budget.

tools.title: Deck Board & Gap Calculator
tools.desc: Straight decking row count with exact board face edges, clear gaps, last rip and explicitly unverified stock-segment joints
tools.formula: Rows = ceil((coverage width+gap)/(actual board width+gap)); final rip = coverage width−(rows−1)×(board+gap); face total=(rows−1)×board width+final rip; clear spaces=(rows−1)×gap; face total+spaces=coverage width. Conservative stock pieces=ceil(rows×ceil(row length/stock length)×(1+waste%)); no offcut reuse, butt-joint support or stock-layout optimization.
tools.example: 120-in coverage, 5.5-in boards, 0.125-in gaps: 22 rows and a 1.875-in final rip. The 21 full faces sum to 115.5 in, plus 1.875 in final rip and 21 × 0.125 in gaps = 120 in total. If stock is shorter than each row, stock count is an ordering reference only, not an approved seam plan.
tools.limit: Straight parallel row quantity and face dimensions only; does NOT check joist alignment or provide a usable butt-joint plan when stock length is shorter than row length. The stock-piece estimate ignores offcut reuse, joist end support, fastening, board expansion, end trim, stagger patterns, tolerance, structural spans and code. Rows with extremely small final rip (<1e-7 in) are rejected. SVG is a schematic, not a physical cutting template. Use Deck Material Estimator for joist-center reference seam planning.

guidance.heading: Verify the last rip and every clear gap
guidance.text: The cut list now includes left and right face positions, physical rip width and the gap following each row. The last row has no following gap. Board-face widths, all inter-row gaps and the last rip must add exactly to the entered coverage.

guidance.heading: Count stock conservatively, not as an approved joint plan
guidance.text: Stock pieces per row = ceiling(row length ÷ stock length). The displayed suggested order applies waste and assumes no offcut reuse. For stock shorter than a run, no joist or attachment positions are provided here: do not treat the quantity as a verified butt-joint layout.

guidance.heading: Compare with the joist-aware tool
guidance.text: For a reference joist grid and allowable seams at those centers, use Deck Material Estimator. Actual joist dimensions, fasteners, staggered ends, edge supports and safe installations still require validation.

tools.title: Baluster & Spindle Spacing
tools.desc: Equal clear baluster gaps and accurate left/right face locations with end-gap and opening-closure verification
tools.formula: Number of balusters = max(1,ceil((clear opening−maximum desired gap)/(actual baluster width+maximum gap))); equal clear gap = (opening−count×face width)/(count+1). Face i spans center±face width/2; all count faces and count+1 gaps must sum to the entered opening.
tools.example: 96 in clear opening, 1.5 in faces and maximum 4 in clear gap yield 17 balusters and 18 gaps at 3.916666… in each; 17×1.5 + 18×3.916666… = 96 in. Each face has its own left/right coordinates.
tools.limit: A mathematical straight-run spacing reference only, NOT a baluster safety-code certificate. The selected maximum gap may not match local requirements, particularly for stairs or children. Faces are measured perpendicular to the opening; actual rails, attachments, posts, rail slope, compliance and finished clearances require independent verification. Zero clear gap is mathematically possible but may be unusable. SVG and printed schematics are not 1:1 templates.

guidance.heading: Use the actual clear opening
guidance.text: Enter the unobstructed inside-face span between the two supporting post/rail boundaries and the measured face width of one baluster. Maximum gap means the upper limit of the OPEN gap, not the center pitch.

guidance.heading: Check both boundary gaps and every baluster face
guidance.text: The equal gap appears before the first face, between neighboring faces, and after the last face. Each exported record gives center, physical left/right face edges and clear gap to the next; the full sum must close to the clear opening.

guidance.heading: Confirm safety and installation outside this calculator
guidance.text: Actual railing compliance depends on the local code, real materials, slope/angle, attachment system and approved gauge. A numeric gap at or below the selected maximum is not a safety approval.

tools.title: Common Rafter & Birdsmouth Cut Layout
tools.desc: Ridge-adjusted common rafter, eave length and measurable birdsmouth horizontal seat/vertical heel cut endpoints with HAP.
tools.formula: Adjusted horizontal run = entered ridge-centerline run−ridge thickness/2; face slope=pitch/12; rise=adjusted run×slope; rafter reference line=hypot(adjusted run,rise); slope tail=hypot(horizontal overhang,horizontal overhang×slope). Total slope to tail=sum. Horizontal birdsmouth seat span has nominal vertical rise=seat×slope and perpendicular notch depth=seat×sin(atan(slope)); remaining normal stock depth=stock depth−notch depth. True 2D cut datum: X is horizontal from the ridge top toward the eave, Y is vertically DOWN from the ridge top. At bearing OUTSIDE wall-face x=adjusted run R, stock lower edge y=(pitch/12)×x + D×sqrt(1+(pitch/12)²), with D entered NORMAL to the sloping roof. The seat begins at (R−seat,lowerY(R−seat)) and ends at (R,same Y); the heel plumb cut ends at (R,lowerY(R)). HAP (vertical top at bearing to seat surface)=D×sqrt(1+slope²)−seat×slope. Notch face area=0.5×seat×heel vertical length. The schematic uses PLUMB reference end clips, not certified cut contours or a full-length saw jig.
tools.example: At 6:12 and horizontal ridge-centerline run 120 in with no ridge board, the common rafter to bearing is 134.16408 in with 60 in rise, matching Roof Pitch for 120 in. With 1.5 in ridge thickness, run reduces to 119.25 in, rise to 59.625 in and ridge-to-bearing length≈133.3256 in. A 12-in horizontal overhang adds 13.4164 in of slope line. Actual plumb/seat cuts are not certified. For a 6:12 pitched 5.5-in deep rafter with a 3-in seat, the vertical heel cut is 1.5 in, normal notch 1.34164079 in, HAP approximately 4.64918694 in and remaining normal throat 4.15835921 in. Reference coordinates and numeric CSV identify the precise two modeled cut segments. These are NOT validated plate-bearing or structural dimensions.
tools.limit: Exact 2D idealized birdsmouth seat and heel cut reference coordinates are calculated for a square-ended level seat, vertical plumb heel, and the user-entered wall outside-face datum. The modeled plumb-clipped side section is NOT verified against real stock end joinery, minimum bearing/fastener edge distances or overcut tolerances. This calculator does not determine member load rating, permissible code notch fraction, actual top-plate width, ridge connection, framing safety, blade kerf, actual stock defects, field fit or a 1:1 printing template. At zero roof pitch/seat no material-removing birdsmouth is represented.

guidance.heading: Use one roof-face pitch datum across the calculators
guidance.text: A common rafter rises p inches for each 12 inches of horizontal plan run, the same convention as Roof Pitch. The actual adjusted run to the ridge-board face is the original centerline run less half the ridge thickness. Zero ridge allowance gives the same reference run, rise and slope length as Roof Pitch.

guidance.heading: Do not confuse the slope tail with bearing-to-ridge length
guidance.text: The overhang is a horizontal eave projection; it adds its own rise and sloping line to the rafter. The bearing point is kept separate from the tail point in the coordinate schedule, and an independent total horizontal-to-tail dimension is shown.

guidance.heading: Differentiate seat length and notch depth
guidance.text: The horizontal seat is measured INWARD from the wall outside-face plumb datum by the entered seat length. Its end is on that plumb line, and the perpendicular notch penetration is seat×sin(arctan(pitch/12)); the cut heel vertical height is seat×(pitch/12). The rendered side section and coordinate CSV use the same computed end points. At zero slope these cut lengths collapse to no material-removing notch. Positive remaining wood is a geometric condition, not structural acceptance.

guidance.heading: Verify real lumber and roofing requirements
guidance.text: Real plumb cut, ridge connection, bearing, stock depth, permissible notch area, uplift and gravity loads require actual site and code verification. The diagram is proportional within the SVG but is NOT a 1:1 saw/cutting template.

guidance.heading: Read seat, heel and HAP coordinates from the same model
guidance.text: Take X horizontally toward the eave from the ridge top, and Y vertically DOWN from that ridge datum. The chosen outside wall-face PLUMB line lies at the ridge-adjusted run. Horizontal seat begins at (run−seat, lower sloped edge at that station), joins the wall line at constant Y, then the vertical heel cut reaches the unnotched lower edge. HAP is the vertical distance from the wall-line roof top to the seat cut. The numeric CSV and SVG use identical endpoints; the raw board and real building bearing are not certified.

tools.title: Crown Molding Compound Cuts
tools.desc: Compound angle magnitudes and explicit inside/outside, left/right illustrative references with a typed CSV angle schedule
tools.formula: Geometric flat-saw angle magnitudes only: miter = atan(sin(spring)/tan(included wall corner/2)); bevel = asin(cos(spring)×cos(included wall corner/2)). An illustrative plan-view sign changes with inside/outside and left/right selection; this sign is NOT a calibrated saw-control setting.
tools.example: 38° spring angle with a 90° included wall corner gives a 31.62° miter magnitude and a 33.86° bevel magnitude. Inside/outside and left/right change only the illustrative plan sign, not these geometric magnitudes.
tools.limit: Angles are idealized geometric magnitudes under the stated spring/included-corner convention. The signed plan view is illustrative ONLY and must not be used as a prescribed miter-saw left/right, flip, face-up/down or fence placement. Saw brand scales, crown orientation, inside/outside cut direction, relief/back bevel, joint tolerance and physical jig settings require independent hands-on scrap verification.

guidance.heading: Use the included wall angle and the stated spring convention
guidance.text: The entered corner angle is measured between adjacent walls on the selected side. The spring angle is treated as the nominal crown-to-wall spring convention used in the displayed formulas. Check the actual profile and installation orientation before using the computed magnitudes.

guidance.heading: Separate angle magnitudes from saw direction
guidance.text: Miter magnitude and bevel magnitude remain the same when you choose left/right or inside/outside. The optional signed miter only changes an illustrative plan-view sketch and CSV reference. It is NOT a saw rotation command; real hand, crown orientation and tool setup vary.

guidance.heading: Export angles with unambiguous units
guidance.text: The angle schedule includes the selected corner type and piece hand, spring and wall angle, both magnitudes and the signed illustration angle, all in degrees. Switching in/mm does not change any angles.

guidance.heading: Cut a verified sample before processing stock
guidance.text: Confirm the actual saw, crown bedding, surface face, fence orientation and corner geometry with scrap pieces. This tool does not certify safe saw operation, fit, hold-down methods or cutting accuracy.

tools.title: Soffit Drop & Eave Section
tools.desc: Datum-labelled eave section: roof fall, rafter underside, lining and signed fascia adjustment with a proportional cross-section
tools.formula: Roof-top fall = horizontal eave projection × pitch/12. Vertical separation of parallel roof faces = rafter normal depth × √(1+(pitch/12)²). Finished soffit reference drop from the wall rafter-top datum = roof fall + vertical rafter separation + lining vertical thickness + signed fascia adjustment (down positive).
tools.example: At 24 in projection and 6:12 pitch, roof-top fall is 12 in. With a 5.5 in normal rafter depth, 0.5 in lining and zero offset, the vertical rafter separation is 6.1492 in and the finished reference drop is 18.6492 in.
tools.limit: Reference datum is the TOP of the rafter at the wall; positive vertical values point DOWN. Rafter depth is perpendicular to its slope; lining thickness is specified vertically; fascia adjustment is a signed downward-positive additive offset. The diagram models these reference surfaces, not eave framing, structural load, material fastening or a 1:1 cutting template. Actual fascia/soffit assemblies may use different planes and must be field checked.

guidance.heading: Start from a defined wall reference datum
guidance.text: The zero-height line is the top face of the rafter at the wall reference. The nominal pitch fall is measured vertically from this datum to the top rafter surface at the outer eave, for the horizontal projection entered.

guidance.heading: Convert normal rafter depth into a vertical face difference
guidance.text: The rafter depth is measured square to the roof slope, not vertically. Parallel surfaces separated by normal stock depth d have vertical difference d×√(1+slope²) at the same horizontal station. At a 6:12 pitch this exceeds d by about 11.8%.

guidance.heading: Apply lining thickness and the signed fascia datum separately
guidance.text: The finished soffit reference adds the stated vertical lining thickness and the signed fascia adjustment to the eave underside drop. Positive adjustment means farther down; a negative adjustment raises the reference. The exact physical reference plane of a real fascia/soffit assembly must be checked on site.

guidance.heading: Use dimensioned numbers, not the printed SVG as a cutting template
guidance.text: The line drawing illustrates the same numeric datum relationships shown in the results and the two-row CSV. It does not dimension the roof from framing grade, promise local code suitability, provide vertical load-bearing recommendations or certify paper-scale cuts.

tools.title: Kerf Bending Layout
tools.desc: Kerf-bending flat-stock trial plan with continuous-web and nonoverlap checks, saw-mouth extents and a depth-profile drawing
tools.formula: Developed reference arc length = radius×angle (radians). Idealized closure per cut = 2×atan(kerf width/(2×cut depth)); cut depth = stock thickness−retained web. Proposed cuts = ceil(target angle/estimated closure); center spacing = reference arc length/count; clear land = spacing−kerf width. Continuous web and clear land must both be positive.
tools.example: 100 mm reference radius and 90° target gives 157.08 mm developed arc. For a 0.75 in stock with 0.125 in continuous web and 0.125 in saw kerf, 8 proposed cuts give about 19.63 mm pitch; the idealized model does not guarantee final wood curvature.
tools.limit: Geometry-only idealized slit closure, NOT a verified wood-bending, neutral-axis or springback model. Radius is a user-selected reference arc, not a guaranteed finished inside/outer radius. Retained web must be positive; flat kerf mouths must remain separate. Wood species, grain, fatigue, tear-out, saw accuracy and actual bending require scrap trials. SVG/print are scaled schematics, NOT certified 1:1 saw templates.

guidance.heading: Reference arc does not guarantee finished bend radius
guidance.text: The flat layout length is reference radius × bend angle in radians. Real curvature depends on material and the retained continuous web; the neutral axis and finished inside/outer radius are not calculated.

guidance.heading: Preserve a connected web and separate kerf mouths
guidance.text: Each cut stops at the continuous remaining web. Zero web would sever the board and is rejected. If adjacent kerf mouth openings touch or overlap on the flat stock, the suggested layout is rejected instead of generating unusable cut coordinates.

guidance.heading: Distinguish closure estimate from intended turn
guidance.text: Idealized maximum closure per cut is 2×atan(kerf width/(2×cut depth)). The number of cuts rounds up to meet the requested angle; planned average turn per cut = target angle/count, which can be smaller than the estimated maximum closure. Neither predicts springback.

guidance.heading: Inspect the slot profile and trial on scrap
guidance.text: The schedule exports each cut center, two slot mouth edges, depth, retained wood and maximum closure estimate. The flat-stock SVG shows cut mouths above the continuous web and is not a real-scale cutting template. Verify all dimensions and bending behavior on sacrificial stock first.

tools.title: Wainscoting Panel Layout
tools.desc: Equal-width wainscot panel cuts with exact left/right edges, visible gaps, symmetric end margins and dimensional closure
tools.formula: Panel width = (wall width−2×end margin−(panel count−1)×inter-panel gap)/panel count; panel i left = margin+i×(panel width+gap); right = left+panel width. The last panel right must equal wall width−margin; across-wall total = panel faces+all gaps+two end margins.
tools.example: 120 in wall, 5 panels, 3 in end margins and 2 in between-panel gaps: each panel is 21.2 in wide, with positions 3–24.2, 26.2–47.4, 49.4–70.6, 72.6–93.8, and 95.8–117 in. Five faces total 106 in + four gaps total 8 in + two margins total 6 in = 120 in.
tools.limit: Flat straight-wall reference only; does not subtract door/window openings, outlets, skirting, rails, stile thickness, scribe/expansion gaps or trim overhang. Inputs are panel face widths and open between-panel gaps; zero gap means adjoining panels. The drawing and CSV show the same rounded reference edges (1e-8 in coordinate resolution), but are not certified 1:1 paper cutting templates. Verify wall irregularity and finished stock at site.

guidance.heading: Measure clear wall width and symmetric side margins
guidance.text: Enter the length along the wall to cover with equal-width panel faces. The margin is the reserved face clearance at EACH end; the gap appears only between adjacent panels, so one panel has no inter-panel gap.

guidance.heading: Check every right edge before cutting
guidance.text: The schedule lists left and right edges, actual width, panel height and gap after each panel. Each panel ends before the next begins by exactly the entered gap (within coordinate display rounding). End margins, total panel width and combined gaps must add back to the measured wall width.

guidance.heading: Diagram follows schedule edges, not a styled minimum width
guidance.text: The SVG now plots the same left/right numeric endpoints as the schedule, including narrow panels and zero gaps, instead of drawing all narrow panels as if at least one pixel wide. The wall outline is schematic in vertical height only.

guidance.heading: Use actual finished stock sizes
guidance.text: This is a face-layout and cut-reference calculator, not a door/window takeoff or a construction fastening guide. Actual trims, stile overlaps, wall deviations, adhesive/fastener placement and fabrication tolerances require separate checks.

tools.title: Straight Stair Calculator
tools.desc: Calculate straight stair riser heights, tread layout, proportional elevation and total footprint including optional upper landing depth.
tools.formula: risers = ceil(total rise / desired maximum riser); actual riser height = total rise / risers; treads = risers − 1 because upper finished landing is the last walking surface; flight run = treads × tread run; total horizontal footprint = flight run + optional upper landing reference depth.
tools.example: 105 in total rise with 7.5 in desired maximum and 10 in tread run gives 14 equal 7.5 in risers, 13 treads, 130 in flight run. Add a separately measured 36 in upper landing for a 166 in reference footprint.
tools.limit: Straight-flight geometry only: measured total rise is between finished floor walking elevations; treads = risers − 1 assumes the upper landing is the last walking surface. Optional landing depth extends the horizontal footprint beyond the last riser but is NOT an extra tread. This does not verify code minima, headroom, handrails, stair widths, tread nosing, actual landing dimensions, structural capacity or stringer cuts. Verify site geometry and local regulations.

guidance.heading: Count actual risers from total vertical rise
guidance.text: Measure floor-to-floor rise using the intended finished walking surfaces. Enter a positive desired maximum riser height: the calculator rounds the number of risers up, then divides the total rise equally among them. This means the displayed actual riser can be shorter than the requested maximum.

guidance.heading: Why tread count is one less than riser count
guidance.text: For this straight-flight convention, the upper finished floor is the final walking surface, so 14 risers correspond to 13 distinct horizontal treads. The flight's horizontal run is those 13 tread runs. The independently entered optional upper landing depth begins at the final rise and adds to the total reference footprint; it does not change riser or tread count.

guidance.heading: When to use the more detailed stringer tool
guidance.text: This is a layout arithmetic check, not an approval of stair geometry, handrails or building-code limits. Use the separate Stair Stringer Calculator for a reference cutting schedule that considers tread thickness and lower-floor correction. Verify finished heights and local requirements before construction.

guidance.heading: Use the individual tread and riser coordinate schedule
guidance.text: The schedule lists each riser elevation, its horizontal position, the next tread's start/end coordinates and which surface is the upper landing. Zero is the first riser's horizontal datum; all positions increase toward the upper landing. Export in inches or switch to millimeters without changing the measured geometry. The SVG uses the same coordinates and scale, but is not a full-size cutting template.

tools.title: Rise & Run Slope Converter
tools.desc: Convert a measured vertical rise and horizontal run into slope angle, true diagonal length, pitch per 12 and percent grade.
tools.formula: slope=rise/run; angle=atan(slope); length=hypot(rise,run)
tools.limit: Run must be nonzero

guidance.heading: Use actual horizontal run, not diagonal length
guidance.text: Enter the vertical height change as Rise and the horizontal projection as Run. The slope length is the hypotenuse computed from those two legs. Entering an already-sloped tape-measure length as Run would overstate the diagonal result.

guidance.heading: Compare pitch, degrees and percent grade
guidance.text: Pitch per 12 is 12 times rise divided by run, while grade is 100 times the same ratio. The angle comes from atan2(rise,run), converted to degrees. For example, a 36-inch rise over 72 inches of horizontal run is 6:12, 50% grade and approximately 26.565 degrees.

guidance.heading: Zero rise and unsupported layouts
guidance.text: A horizontal reference with zero rise is valid and yields zero angle, but the run must be positive. This is a right-triangle converter, not a structural roof or stair design; use Rafter Calculator for ridge and birdsmouth references when those dimensions matter.

tools.title: Deck Material Estimator
tools.desc: Deck board cut lengths, measured butt-end gaps, joist-face overlap references, fastener quantities and purchasing estimates.

inputs.label: Purchased decking board unit price (0 = unquoted)
Fasteners per piece / joist contact (0 = exclude)
Clear gap between decking board ends at butt seams
Measured joist top face width under each butt seam
Required horizontal face overlap PER board end (0 = no threshold)

tools.formula: Rows = ceil((coverage+gap)/(board face width+gap)); final rip = coverage−(rows−1)×(face width+gap). With given joist center references (0, OC, …, end), each board segment ends at the farthest joist center reachable within purchased stock length, unless the final deck end is reachable. Every supported piece consumes one stock board; no offcut reuse or seam staggering. Fastening contact count = decking rows × (joist references + number of butt seams per row), counting each of the TWO stock pieces at a shared butt seam separately. Requested fasteners = fastening contacts × user-entered fasteners per contact; supplier packs = ceil(requested fasteners / supplier pack size). Decking purchase cost = (stock boards with allowance) × per-board quote; fastener purchase cost = packs × pack quote. A 0 price means NOT QUOTED, never free stock. Costs only total once every needed component has a quote. Optional seam end gap g splits board-end cuts around each measured joist CENTER (x): first end x-g/2, next start x+g/2. For face width w, nominal equal end-face overlap=(w-g)/2; physical cut lengths plus joint gaps must equal row deck lengths.
tools.example: For a 120 × 144 in deck using 5.5 in boards and 0.125 in gaps, 16 in joist centers and 100 in stock: 22 rows with a 1.875 in final rip each receive a 96 in and 48 in segment, joined at the 96 in joist center reference. This gives 44 stock boards before allowance, not a 100 in/44 in unsupported joint.
tools.limit: Rectangular straight-deck reference geometry only. Segment butt joints are constrained to entered joist CENTERLINES, not validated bearing widths, joint reinforcement, double-joist blocking or fastening. All rows use identical, UNSTAGGERED joints as a conservative reference, not an approved construction pattern. No offcut reuse, structural span approval, load rating, end gap, board defects, ledger design or footing calculations. Fastener quantities are a user-controlled arithmetic planning assumption, not a prescribed fastening pattern or building-code recommendation. Each butt seam creates two piece-to-joist contacts on the same single joist centerline; this does not verify that the joist can actually bear both ends. The board segment estimate does not charge saw kerf, trimming, defects, delivery or tax; no joist lumber purchasing estimate is made. Currency is a label only with no automatic exchange conversion. Alternate seam mode is only a measured joist-CENTER proposal; different seam stations are reported only when actually obtained. No butt joint support or staggered installation pattern is structurally approved. Optional positive butt gap uses square board-end cuts centered about the measured joist face. Joist-face overlap is a flat 1D geometric quantity, not rated bearing: lateral placement, actual fastening, edge-distance, blocking, material grade and local requirements must be reviewed on site.

guidance.heading: Boards and joist reference grid
guidance.text: Deck width runs across parallel decking rows; deck length runs along them. Joist centers begin at zero, follow your chosen OC spacing and end with a potentially shorter last bay. Enter actual face width and purchased stock length, not nominal lumber sizes.

guidance.heading: Every butt seam must have a reference center
guidance.text: Unlike simple stock-length division, this calculator places every intermediate board end at the furthest joist center that can be reached within one purchased board. If there is no such joist center and stock will not span to the deck end, the tool rejects the layout rather than inventing an unsupported butt seam. The SVG marks each proposed seam and the CSV exports butt-joint coordinates.

guidance.heading: Layout reference, NOT a fastening or stagger plan
guidance.text: The reference repeats the same seams across all rows and does not stagger joints. A single joist centerline does not establish sufficient edge bearing for two board ends; joist width, double-joist/blocking support, end gaps, fastening, local rules and safe maximum joist span must be reviewed separately. Counts are conservative without offcut reuse.

guidance.heading: How fastening contacts are counted at butt seams
guidance.text: At each entered joist-center reference, every independent decking piece touching that line is counted once. A row with no butt seams has one contact per joist line. A single proposed butt seam causes TWO separate pieces to contact that same joist reference, so it adds one more contact per row. Multiply the resulting contacts by your own assumed number of fasteners per piece/contact, or enter zero to exclude hardware.

guidance.heading: Build a supplier-priced board and fastener order
guidance.text: Enter your actual price per purchased decking stock board and per fastener pack, along with fasteners per contact and pack size. The calculator includes separately rounded board reserve stock, whole-pack hardware purchases and partial-price warnings. Enter 0 for an unavailable quote rather than claiming a free material. The price currency selector only changes the displayed label; it does not convert the entered values.

guidance.heading: What the materials budget intentionally excludes
guidance.text: This is a nonstructural reference purchase estimate for decking pieces and selected fastener packs only. The joist lines are user-entered CENTER references, not designed joists; their width, bearing, spans, blocking, hangers, structural attachments, end trimming and extra fastening at supported edges are unverified. Physically validate the proposed joints, real lumber lengths and manufacturer installation instructions before purchasing.

guidance.heading: Alternate butt seams without inventing support locations
guidance.text: The optional alternate seam mode calculates both left-to-right and right-to-left seam chains on the user-entered joist CENTER grid. Odd-numbered rows use the original forward chain; even-numbered rows use the reverse chain. Every cut must fit the stock length. If both chains have the same seams, a stagger cannot be guaranteed. The report counts rows with truly different seam stations, not just the selected mode. Do not treat either pattern as a certified joint-support design; blocking, joist face width and local fastening remain excluded.

guidance.heading: Physical board ends around each butt seam
guidance.text: The optional butt-end clear gap defaults to zero so historical centerline layouts remain unchanged. If a positive gap is entered, each joist-center seam x creates two true board cut faces at x−gap/2 and x+gap/2. Each cut-list row includes its physical start and length, with the end coordinate added when the gap is enabled. Length conservation includes all clear gaps.

guidance.heading: Measure joist support face and check overlap
guidance.text: Enter the ACTUAL top face width, not nominal lumber size. If a butt joint is centered on that joist face, each board end has (face width−end gap)/2 of horizontal geometric face overlap. An optional user-entered minimum can reject the measured layout, but does not validate bearing strength, edge fastener distance, blocking, span or any code-approved installation. Real butt joints require qualified physical verification.

tools.title: Segmented Bowl Ring Calculator
tools.desc: Tapered polygon rings, per-ring miter cuts, accurate chord faces, stack heights and optional rough stock allowances with numeric SVG/CSV exports.

inputs.label: Outer corner diameter change per next ring (signed)
Inner corner diameter change per next ring (signed)
One kerf allowance per blank axis

tools.formula: Half-miter=180°/n; outer/inner chord=D×sin(π/n). Radial end-face length=(outerD−innerD)/2, but perpendicular trapezoid face depth=radial length×cos(π/n). The largest ideal turned circular OD fitting the OUTER polygon is outer corner diameter×cos(π/n); chord faces are straight. For ring i (zero based), outer/inner corner diameter = base diameter + i×signed step. Nominal stack elevation = i×entered layer height. Reference rough rectangular blank length=outer chord+2×edge allowance+one kerf; rough blank width=perpendicular face depth+2×edge allowance+one kerf. This is an explicit conservative estimating convention, not optimized sawing.
tools.example: 12 in outer CORNER diameter, 8 in inner CORNER diameter, 12 segments: 15° half-miter, 3.10583 in outer and 2.07055 in inner chords, 2 in radial end face, 1.93185 in perpendicular face depth. Ideal round OD limit is 11.59111 in, not 12 in.
tools.limit: Inputs are corner-to-corner polygon envelope diameters, NOT guaranteed finished turned diameters. Face geometry omits saw kerf, joint loss, glue oversize, stock thickness, wood grain, ring staggering, lathe holding and physical allowances. Finished circular outside diameter should stay BELOW the ideal polygon inradius with a real margin. Optional multi-ring steps produce independent polygon envelopes, not a continuous finished profile. Rough blank size is a one-piece rectangular reference with 2-sided user margin plus one entered kerf per axis, not an optimized cutting or purchasing layout.

guidance.heading: Polygon corners are not finished turning diameters
guidance.text: This model measures the outer and inner diameter through polygon VERTICES. The outer edges of every segment are straight chords. The ideal largest round outside surface that fits the outer polygon is corner diameter×cos(180°/segments), before any real trimming or glue and turning allowances.

guidance.heading: Distinguish radial end length and perpendicular board-face depth
guidance.text: The distance along a radial mitered end equals (outer diameter−inner diameter)/2. The perpendicular face depth from the outer straight chord to the inner straight chord is shorter: radial end length×cos(180°/segments). A 12/8 in, 12-piece ring uses a 2 in radial end length but only 1.93185 in chord-to-chord depth; neither includes stock oversize or saw kerf.

guidance.heading: Physical segment schedule and drawing consistency
guidance.text: The SVG uses straight trapezoid polygons, not curved arc pieces. It shows the ideal maximum circular outside diameter as a separate dashed circle. Per-piece CSV exports chord lengths, radial and perpendicular face depths, and geometric face area with typed units. Repeat rings are identical; this does not design a tapered multi-ring bowl profile.

guidance.heading: Design different-sized stacked rings without inventing a finished bowl profile
guidance.text: Enter signed outer and inner polygon corner-diameter changes per successive ring and a nominal layer height. The engine validates every ring, calculates its own cut chords, perpendicular face depth, turning limit and elevation, and exports each physical segment; zero diameter changes keep the original identical-ring workflow. The side preview is a corner-envelope elevation and does not assert actual turned wall thickness or glue deformation.

guidance.heading: Bounded rough blank allowance and saw kerf
guidance.text: The optional allowance adds the entered margin to both sides of the outer-chord length and the perpendicular face-depth width. To make the estimate conservative, the separate entered kerf is charged once to each rough blank axis. This produces individually sized rectangular rough blanks and their sum area, without claiming a minimum stock board size, exact saw sequence, recoverable offcuts or supplier quantity. Measure blade kerf, wood behavior and clamping on actual stock.

tools.title: Roof Pitch in Degrees & Percent
tools.desc: Convert rise per 12 horizontal run into roof-face degrees, grade, vertical rise and true slope-line length
tools.formula: Given pitch p: slope=p/12; angle=atan(slope); percentage grade=100×slope; rise=horizontal run×slope; sloping length=hypot(horizontal run,rise). The 12 is horizontal, not measured along a sloped roof face.
tools.example: At 6:12 with 120 in horizontal face run, rise=60 in, slope-line length≈134.16408 in, angle≈26.56505° and grade=50%. The same rise and line apply to a common rafter with zero ridge deduction and zero overhang; a diagonal hip rafter is different.
tools.limit: Ideal straight roof-face triangle only. No hip-azimuth correction, ridge thickness adjustment, bearing, plumb/saw calibration, roofing code, structure or actual site grade. The SVG is a correctly proportioned geometric reference within its viewport, not a scale-to-print cutting template.

guidance.heading: Pitch is rise over horizontal run
guidance.text: For 6:12, each 12 inches of HORIZONTAL run rises 6 inches. The conversion to angle is atan(6/12), not arcsin(6/12). Grade is 50 percent, but the sloped line length is longer than the run.

guidance.heading: Compare identical datums across tools
guidance.text: Roof Pitch and Common Rafter agree only when Common Rafter's run matches this horizontal reference and ridge thickness and overhang are both set to zero. A ridge board reduces the adjusted common-rafter run by half its actual thickness.

guidance.heading: Hip pitch uses a different horizontal reference
guidance.text: Hip Rafter's face pitch input is still this same common roof-face 6:12. Its elevation angle is based on the hip's PLAN DIAGONAL, which is longer than its across-face run. Do not substitute 26.565° as the hip-line elevation angle.

tools.title: Equal Center Spacing
tools.desc: Place evenly spaced center marks or full-width parts with measured face edges, clear gaps and safe end margins.

inputs.label: Physical part face width (0 = marks only)

tools.formula: For n ≥ 2: center pitch = (total length − left center offset − right center offset)/(n − 1); center i = left offset + i×pitch. For n = 1, center = (left offset + total length − right offset)/2. When part width w > 0: face edges = center ± w/2, clear face gap = pitch − w, and first/last faces must stay inside the measured run.
tools.example: 1000 mm total length, 6 equal parts, 50 mm left/right center offsets, 30 mm physical part width: centers 50, 230, 410, 590, 770, 950 mm; 180 mm center pitch, 150 mm clear face gaps and 35 mm end margins.
tools.limit: All offsets are measured to part centers, not faces. Zero part width means marking centers only, not an infinitely thin physical board. With a positive width, full part faces must fit inside the entered run and adjacent parts must not overlap. Exactly one center is placed midway between offset reference positions; gap is not defined. This does not certify spacing code, safe minimum fastener distances or material deformation.

guidance.heading: Offsets refer to centers, not object edges
guidance.text: The left and right offsets locate the first and last center marks. A positive optional part width allows the calculator to show each physical face interval, actual clear gap between faces, and remaining end margins. Because the offsets still refer to centers, they must be at least half a part width when the outer faces are expected to stay inside the run.

guidance.heading: How equal centers are distributed
guidance.text: For two or more centers, the calculator divides the usable run (total length minus both center offsets) into count minus one equal intervals. The optional physical width does not change these center coordinates; it only derives face edges and gaps. If you request one center, it is placed midway between the two reference offsets, and no between-part gap is reported.

guidance.heading: Transfer the marks without accumulating rounding drift
guidance.text: Export face edges and center coordinates from the same measured datum rather than repeatedly adding a rounded displayed pitch. When physical part width is supplied, the SVG draws rectangles proportional to that width and rejects faces outside the run or overlapping neighbors. Inch fractions are visual guides; CSV exports numeric dimensions in the selected unit.

guidance.heading: Example: six equal-width parts over one meter
guidance.text: For a 1000 mm run with six parts, centers inset 50 mm from both ends and part face widths of 30 mm, the correct pitch is 180 mm, clear gaps are 150 mm and outside clear margins are each 35 mm. This optional face-layout mode is different from the default zero-width center-only mark schedule; it does not design fasteners or structural connections.

tools.title: Hip Rafter Line Geometry
tools.desc: Hip-rafter three-dimensional line from actual plan X/Y runs, roof-face pitch, and separate hip-elevation pitch
tools.formula: Common roof-face slope = (rise-per-12)/12; vertical rise = across-roof plan run × slope. Plan diagonal = hypot(along-roof run, across-roof run). True hip line = hypot(plan diagonal, vertical rise). Plan angle = atan2(across,along); HIP elevation angle = atan2(vertical rise,plan diagonal). Effective HIP rise-per-12 = 12×vertical rise/plan diagonal, which is NOT generally the original roof-face pitch.
tools.example: At common 6:12 roof pitch with 120 in of along-roof and 120 in across-roof run, the plan hip is 169.70563 in, rise is 60 in, true 3D hip length is 180 in, plan angle is 45°, hip elevation angle is about 19.4712° and effective HIP pitch is 4.24264:12. A 6:12 common roof face itself rises at 26.5651°.
tools.limit: Geometry of a line between an eave reference and ridge/hip reference only. Across-run controls rise, NOT plan-diagonal distance; hip elevation angle is different from face pitch. This does not calculate real hip lumber back bevel, side cuts, ridge-width deduction, plumb-cut setting, material thickness, overhang, drop hip, bearing capacity or roof-framing code. SVG gives separate plan and elevation reference triangles at proportionate within-view scales, not a 1:1 cutting jig.

guidance.heading: Keep across-roof pitch separate from the hip diagonal
guidance.text: The 6:12 value is vertical rise for every 12 inches measured ACROSS the common roof face in plan. The hip runs diagonally, so its 3D elevation angle and effective pitch per 12 diagonal-run are shallower, even though the roof face pitch is unchanged.

guidance.heading: Compare the projected and true hip runs
guidance.text: The plan view uses the along-roof and across-roof runs; the projected hypotenuse is the 2D plan diagonal. The elevation view instead uses that diagonal as its horizontal run and the same vertical rise from across-run pitch. These are different triangles with consistent 3D endpoints.

guidance.heading: Read the export as a geometric line reference
guidance.text: The single-row CSV exports along/cross plan runs, roof rise, plan diagonal, true 3D length, plan azimuth and hip elevation angle. It does not provide a bevel/cut schedule. Changing feet, inches, centimeters, millimeters or meters changes lengths but never degrees.

guidance.heading: Check structural/cut geometry separately
guidance.text: An actual hip rafter needs roof-specific ridge/back-bevel, plumb cuts, supports, framing layout and structural sizing. Do not use this diagram as a saw-setting chart, structural approval or printed full-scale template.

tools.title: Hip Roof Sheet Layout Calculator
tools.desc: Four-plane equal-pitch hip-roof sheets with cleaned triangular/trapezoid cuts, exported local and projected vertices, and sheet-by-sheet material conservation

options.label: Conservative: one fresh sheet per installed cut
Try nonrotated stock bounding-box reuse (bounded heuristic)

tools.formula: Equal-pitch hip roof: developed surface factor=sqrt(1+(pitch/12)²). Project each north/south trapezoid and west/east triangle to its actual developed slope plane; clip stock-sheet rectangles against every slope polygon; remove duplicate and redundant collinear vertices. For each occupied sheet: local polygon area + discarded offcut area = original stock face area. Each slope's polygon areas and the combined four-plane area must equal their analytical surfaces; projected plan vertices map to the top-down SVG.
tools.example: A flat 192×96-in rectangular hip roof with 96×48-in sheets (long edge eave-parallel) has a 128-ft² footprint. The four slope surfaces together require six separate stock positions rather than the four-sheet geometric area lower bound; per-piece local cut polygon and projected plan vertices now appear in CSV. Counts assume no offcut reuse.
tools.limit: Geometry-only equal-pitch four-plane roof: planar triangles/trapezoids and developed-surface stock polygon cuts. Cut Vertices are sheet-LOCAL developed-slope coordinates, while Plan Projection Vertices are roof-PLAN coordinates used solely for the diagram, NOT flat cutting shapes. No cross-plane offcut reuse, actual sheathing bearing, fastener design, joint stagger, allowable roof loading, material expansion or building-code approval. Cleaned polygon vertices and areas are reference geometry, not certified 1:1 saw templates. Optional reuse is a bounded no-rotation rectangular BOUNDING-BOX heuristic for at most 400 pieces; all polygon corner scrap is treated as inaccessible. User-entered split-line kerf does not cover actual angled polygon perimeter cutting, safe blade clearance, support framing, fastening, or expansion gaps. Validate physical saw cuts and install before purchase.

guidance.heading: Identify the two different vertex coordinate systems
guidance.text: Cut Vertices are (eave direction, uphill direction) pairs measured from a sheet's own lower-left corner on its developed sloped plane. Each sheet also has a slope-specific Eave Offset and Slope Offset. Plan Projection Vertices are global overhead roof-outline (x,y) coordinates, and those projected points drive the top-down SVG. A projected polygon is NOT the same physical cut shape as a tilted sheet.

guidance.heading: Inspect the diagonal hip cut as a proper polygon
guidance.text: The intersection between a diagonal hip boundary and a stock-sheet cell generates a triangle, quadrilateral or clipped multi-vertex polygon. Duplicate corners and redundant collinear middle points at exact grid intersections are removed, so the cut list no longer contains zero-length edge instructions. Grid row, column, plane name and actual cut polygon vertices identify each piece.

guidance.heading: Check the area of every slope, sheet and discarded offcut
guidance.text: The four separate slope-plane cut areas must match the analytical north/south trapezoid and east/west triangle surfaces. Each occupied sheet uses one original full sheet: reported used cut area plus its unreused stock offcut must equal the original stock face area. The total before any optional allowance is shown separately from installed developed roof area.

guidance.heading: Confirm roof installation independently
guidance.text: The app does not nest triangular scraps from one slope into other positions; counts are conservative. Verify actual roof sheathing support, stagger, nail patterns, allowable gaps, engineered loads, safe access and construction tolerances separately. The SVG is a scaled schematic, not a certified cutting pattern.

guidance.heading: Optional stock offcut assignment is geometrically explicit
guidance.text: An optional bounded layout packs every finished cut's axis-aligned bounding box onto supplier-size sheets, using deterministic nonrotated guillotine splits. Every stock placement exports its own X/Y and polygon vertices relative to the original stock face, with a separate split-line kerf. Used polygon area, inaccessible scrap inside boxes, lost kerf and remaining free stock must equal purchased stock area. This is a feasible geometric arrangement within the chosen assumptions, NOT an optimal layout, bearing approval or verified saw path.

tools.title: Wall Stud Count & Layout
tools.desc: Estimate regular wall stud centers, face positions and nominal stud cut length from spacing, wall height and plate thickness.
tools.formula: Nominal centers = 0, OC multiples below L, and far-end center L. Remove a nominal center if its face overlaps the mandatory end stud. Cut = gross wall height − total plate deduction.
tools.example: 120 in between end stud centers at 16 in OC gives 9 centers; 96 in gross height minus 4.5 in plates gives 91.5 in cut length.
tools.limit: Centerline geometry only. End stud faces extend outside the entered center-to-center run; openings require Framing. Total plate deduction is applied once; verify physical field dimensions.

guidance.heading: Wall length is measured between end stud centers
guidance.text: Place the first nominal stud at center zero and the far-end stud at the entered wall length. Intermediate centers follow the chosen on-center interval, with overlapping near-end faces suppressed. Because this is a center-to-center reference, the outside faces of the end studs extend beyond the entered run.

guidance.heading: Calculate the common vertical cut height
guidance.text: The same nominal stud cut height is used for each member: gross wall height minus one combined plate deduction. The result does not independently measure a bottom and double top plate, so enter their total assumed vertical deduction and verify it against the intended assembly.

guidance.heading: Openings require a different takeoff
guidance.text: This simple straight wall model has no doors or windows. For an opening, use Wall Framing with Doors & Windows, which separately lists king, jack, header, sill and cripple reference members. Neither calculator determines structural capacity or local building-code compliance.

tools.title: Shelf Spacing & Drill Marks
tools.desc: Equalize shelf openings, report each shelf face, and optionally produce verified four-pin support-hole X/Y coordinates for both cabinet side panels.

inputs.label: Support-hole center drop below shelf underside
Support pin hole diameter (0 = no drilling grid)

tools.formula: Free height = interior height − shelves×thickness − top reserve − bottom reserve. Shared base gap = free height/(shelves+1). Actual bottom opening = bottom reserve+base gap; actual top opening = top reserve+base gap; all between-shelf gaps = base gap. Optional drilling model (enabled when pin-hole diameter >0): per shelf pin-center Y = shelf bottom elevation − measured hole-center drop. On EACH cabinet side panel, X positions from the INSIDE FRONT edge = front-center inset and cabinet depth − back-center inset. Repeat front/back positions on both left and right inside side panels (4 holes per shelf). Required clear wood at each panel edge is center distance − hole radius; hole centers must be below the shelf underside and above any prior shelf top. Both X and Y distances are referenced to the same inside-front/bottom corner of each panel.
tools.example: A 40 in interior with three 1 in shelves and 2 in extra bottom and 1 in extra top reserves leaves a shared 8.5 in base gap; actual bottom clear opening is 10.5 in, actual top clear opening 9.5 in. With 40 in inside height, 3 shelves of 1 in thickness, 2 in extra bottom and 1 in extra top reserves: shelf bottoms are 10.5, 20, 29.5 in. A 12 in deep cabinet, 1.5 in front/back insets, 0.25 in hole-center drop and 0.19685 in (approx 5 mm) pin holes yields X centers 1.5 and 10.5 in, Y centers 10.25, 19.75 and 29.25 in. Repeat each pair on both left and right panels for 12 holes total.
tools.limit: Top and bottom inputs are extra minimum-reserve clearances, not the final visible openings. Finished shelf faces and clear gaps follow the supplied interior height and actual material thickness. No shelf-load, fixing, sag or material tolerance assessment. The optional drilled support pattern is OFF until a positive pin-hole diameter is entered, retaining legacy shelf spacing and cut-list exports. Coordinates refer to a reference hole center on each INSIDE side panel, with FRONT at X=0 and cabinet bottom at Y=0; left/right panels share these FRONT-referenced coordinates, not a blind same-edge mirror. Drill-hole diameter and measured drop are NOT supplied by hardware manufacturers: verify the actual shelf pin shape, bearing height, countersinking, plate thickness, side-panel dimensions, shelf clearance and drilling depth before fabrication. The SVG is proportionally scaled, NOT a 1:1 drilling jig or structural attachment design.

guidance.heading: Reserved versus actual end clearances
guidance.text: The top and bottom inputs reserve minimum space. Remaining free height is spread across all spaces. Actual bottom clearance = bottom reserve + shared gap; actual top clearance = top reserve + shared gap. If you need the end openings to be exact values, verify the calculated final openings before construction.

guidance.heading: Measure bottom and top faces from the case floor
guidance.text: Every schedule row gives the shelf's bottom and upper surfaces, clear opening below, and clear opening above. All positions reference the inside bottom of the case; board thickness and spacing share the same model.

guidance.heading: Loads and mounting are not sized
guidance.text: This is a geometry-only shelf spacing calculator. It does not recommend material spans, deflection limits, screw spacing, load ratings, wall anchors or fastening methods.

guidance.heading: Optional four-hole-per-shelf support drilling
guidance.text: Enter actual cabinet interior depth, measured front and back hole-center insets, vertical pin-hole center drop below each shelf underside, and the intended drill diameter. A zero diameter disables all support holes while preserving the original shelf-position worksheet. A positive diameter generates exactly two front/back center holes per shelf on each of the two side panels; both side panels use X from the inside FRONT edge and Y from the cabinet's inside bottom.

guidance.heading: Verify the shelf underside versus hardware center
guidance.text: A metal pin's hole-center elevation depends on the real pin/support head design, not on the shelf thickness alone. Measure the vertical difference between shelf underside and required drilling center, then enter that as the drop. The calculator requires every drilled circle to fit entirely below its associated shelf underside, above the previous shelf's top surface, and inside the left/right panel's front/back boundaries. This geometric validation is not proof of the pin load rating.

guidance.heading: Use the separate side-panel drill plan and CSV
guidance.text: The side-panel plan plots depth along X and height along Y on one physical drawing scale, then duplicates the exact front/back coordinates for Left and Right panels. The table exports each shelf number, panel name, front/back position and hole X/Y center and circular edges. Exporting, zooming and printing this reference does not certify the printer's scale, face drilling depth, panel orientation or manufacturer mounting instructions.

tools.title: Gable Roof Area Calculator
tools.desc: Estimate two-plane gable roof surface area, pitched half-span rise and sloped length with one uniform eave overhang.
tools.formula: line=hypot(halfspan,halfspan×pitch/12); area=2×line×effective length
tools.example: A symmetric gable has two matching roof planes
tools.limit: Dormers, valleys and waste excluded

guidance.heading: Define the symmetric roof footprint
guidance.text: Width is the building's full horizontal span; length runs parallel to the ridge. The calculator assumes two matching roof planes and adds the same horizontal overhang to each eave side and to both ends of the building. It does not support different overhangs on the four sides.

guidance.heading: How the total sloped area is calculated
guidance.text: Each half-plane uses horizontal run equal to half the building width plus the overhang. Multiply that run by the entered pitch per 12 to get rise; the sloped length is the right-triangle hypotenuse. Two times that sloped length times effective roof length produces the displayed area.

guidance.heading: Area is not a purchased sheet takeoff
guidance.text: This result is an idealized surface area with no waste, dormers, skylights or valleys removed. It does not place sheets on a grid, compute actual cuts, or specify fasteners. Use Roof Sheathing Calculator for a separate reference sheet-layout task and check real roof conditions before ordering.

tools.title: Square Layout Diagonal Checker
tools.desc: Compare both measured diagonals with the Pythagorean target and each other using your own stated measurement tolerance
tools.formula: Ideal right-angle diagonal = √(width²+length²). Signed A/B errors = measured A/B−ideal. Measured diagonal spread = |A−B|. Compare each absolute error and the measured spread separately with your entered tolerance; all three must be within tolerance for the check to pass. Equal diagonals alone cannot prove four right angles without independently checking sides and geometry.
tools.example: For a target 36 × 48 in rectangle, the ideal diagonal is 60 in. If diagonal A is 59.875 in and B is 60 in with a 0.125 in tolerance, each diagonal and their 0.125 in spread meet the stated measurement checks. This does NOT prove all four corners are square.
tools.limit: Geometry-based measurement comparison only, not an actual corner-angle reconstruction, structural survey, calibrated uncertainty estimate or proof of perpendicularity. The SVG shows the IDEAL target rectangle and its two target diagonals, not the measured shape. Even perfectly equal measured diagonals do not establish squareness unless all four edges, opposite-side relationships, planarity and corners are separately validated. User tolerance is not a building-code requirement or automatic construction approval.

guidance.heading: Measure the intended width and length independently
guidance.text: The target diagonal is the Pythagorean length of an ideal right-angle rectangle using your entered width and length. Measure actual edge lengths at the relevant endpoints; a diagonal test by itself cannot establish the side lengths or prove that the corners are square.

guidance.heading: Compare both diagonals, not only their difference
guidance.text: Each measured diagonal is checked against the ideal. The tool also checks the absolute difference between the two measured diagonals. Two equally wrong diagonals can match each other but still differ substantially from the target; they must not be reported as an acceptable square layout.

guidance.heading: Choose a realistic tolerance for your measurement method
guidance.text: The tolerance is an absolute length entered by you, not an inferred code standard. The screen gives a separate Within/Outside result for A, B and their spread. An exact boundary equal to tolerance counts as within. If any check is outside, remeasure the sides, endpoints and diagonals before further layout.

guidance.heading: Treat the picture as the ideal layout, not a measured deformation
guidance.text: The proportional SVG shows a theoretical rectangle with both reference diagonals. It intentionally cannot infer the real corner angles or distorted quadrilateral from these four dimensions. Verify edge lengths and squareness using independent physical techniques on site.

tools.title: Diagonal Brace Calculator
tools.desc: True-scale diagonal brace centerline with along-the-brace end setbacks, exact X/Y cut endpoint coordinates, CSV schedule and proportional SVG.

inputs.label: Setback along brace from each end

tools.formula: Full diagonal = hypot(horizontal, vertical). Unit direction = (horizontal,vertical)/full diagonal. Cut endpoints = unit direction × setback and × (full−setback); cut length = full−2×setback; angle = atan2(vertical,horizontal).
tools.example: 36 in horizontal × 48 in vertical ⇒ 60 in full centerline. With 5 in trimmed from EACH end along the brace: cut length 50 in; start (3,4) in, finish (33,44) in; cut projections 30 in horizontal and 40 in vertical.
tools.limit: The X/Y points describe the brace CENTERLINE relative to the original lower-left datum. No timber face width, actual saw bevel, joint geometry, stock allowance, grain or structural load design is modeled. SVG is scaled for viewing, not a 1:1 template.

guidance.heading: Understand the measurement datum
guidance.text: Horizontal and vertical dimensions locate the original centerline from (0,0) to (width,height). The setback is a measured distance ALONG that diagonal from each original end, not a horizontal or vertical clearance. The worksheet gives both trimmed centerline endpoint coordinates relative to that same datum.

guidance.heading: Check cut coordinates and export
guidance.text: For a 36×48 in original brace with 5 in of setback per end, the cut endpoints are (3,4) in and (33,44) in, leaving 50 in of usable centerline. CSV fields retain numeric X/Y and along-line station values with explicit units. The green SVG line uses exactly those exported points.

guidance.heading: Centerline is not a physical board cut
guidance.text: No real timber breadth, end-bearing profile, bevel, connector position or stock allowance is known. The measured endpoint coordinates are layout references only, and the on-screen diagram is not a paper-scale saw guide. Check the actual joint and material before cutting.

tools.title: Hole Spacing Drilling Guide
tools.desc: Lay out one or multiple aligned drilling rows with measured board length and width, full X/Y center coordinates, true circular hole edges and checked end/side margins.
tools.formula: Along length: x pitch = (length−2×end center setback)/(holes per row−1); x centers = end setback + column×x pitch. Across width: when drilling one row, y center = board width/2; for two or more rows, y pitch=(board width−2×outer-row center setback)/(row count−1) and y centers=outer-row setback + row×y pitch. For each hole of diameter d: circle edges are x±d/2 and y±d/2. Longitudinal clear material = x pitch−d; transverse clear material = y pitch−d; physical end and side margins subtract half the diameter from the corresponding center offsets. Total holes = holes per row × row count.
tools.example: 100 mm board length, 40 mm face width, four 5 mm diameter holes per row, 5 mm end-center setback and 3 drilling rows with 5 mm outer-row center setback: X centers 5,35,65,95 mm; Y centers 5,20,35 mm; 12 holes total. Along-row clearance is 25 mm, between-row clearance is 10 mm, and all four board-edge margins are 2.5 mm. For a single row, Y is automatically centered at 20 mm, regardless of the unused outer-row setback input.
tools.limit: Aligned rectangular grid only, measured from one common left/bottom board corner in the flat face plane. Single-row Y is always centered; the crosswise setback applies only when two or more rows are selected. Circular-hole overlap is rejected along both axes. The entire board face width must be entered and at least one hole diameter wide; physical margins account for the hole radius. No staggered or angled rows, drill-bit runout, countersink diameter, material tear-out, grain direction, load strength, workholding or physical printer scaling is checked. The SVG is proportional geometry, never a 1:1 drill template.

guidance.heading: Choose one row or an aligned drilling grid
guidance.text: Enter the number of holes PER ROW and the number of drilling rows separately. With one row, all hole centers sit halfway across the entered board face width; this maintains the old longitudinal layout without inventing a second row. With two or more rows, both outside rows are located by the crosswise center setback and the intermediate rows are evenly distributed. All rows have the same column X positions.

guidance.heading: Center setbacks are not leftover wood margins
guidance.text: The longitudinal end-center setback and transverse outer-row center setback are measurements to hole centers, not to hole edges. The actual clear wood at each end or side equals the corresponding center setback minus half the drill diameter. A single centered row has equal side margins of half the board width minus half the drill diameter. Setbacks that allow any hole circle to extend past the board edge are rejected.

guidance.heading: Reject overlapping drills in either direction
guidance.text: For an aligned grid, the center distance between adjacent holes in one row is the longitudinal pitch, while the center distance between rows is their transverse pitch. Subtract the diameter from each pitch to obtain clear material. The calculator rejects negative clearance in either direction and also limits total displayed drill coordinates so large grids do not overwhelm a browser or a workshop CSV.

guidance.heading: Transfer full X and Y coordinates from one corner
guidance.text: Use the exported table to find each hole center X measured from the board's left end and Y measured from its bottom side. Every circle has matching left/right and bottom/top hole extents, making the opposite face margins directly checkable. The SVG draws all circles and the board rectangle with one shared X/Y scale; it is a proportional planning view and must not be treated as an actual-size paper drill jig.

tools.title: Straight Stair Stringer Cut Reference
tools.desc: Straight stair nominal sawline coordinates, end-cut reference geometry, stock-axis envelope, scaled drawings and unit-aware cutting schedules.

inputs.label: Extra stock length along grain at EACH end

tools.formula: Riser height = total finished-floor rise/risers; treads=risers−1; horizontal run=treads×tread run. The notch pitch line from first tread at (0,riser height) to upper landing at (run,total rise) measures hypot(run,treads×riser height). The different floor datum diagonal measures hypot(run,total rise) and is NOT a stringer cut length. Notch penetration=step rise×tread run/hypot(step rise,tread run); nominal throat=board normal depth−notch penetration; bottom trim=step rise−tread thickness+additional lower finish. Optional tread nosing is a nonstructural HORIZONTAL projection toward the downhill side from each riser's vertical line, modeled as x(start)−nosing; it does not alter notch pitch, tread count or stringer cutting vertices. Optional upper landing reference depth starts after final riser and adds to the displayed horizontal footprint, not to the notched stringer cut length. Modeled section: slope m = riser height / tread run; nominal upper pitch line is y=m*x + riser height; a parallel lower reference edge at stock normal depth D is y=m*x + riser height − D*sqrt(1+m²). Joining the exact repeated notch vertices to this lower edge at the FIRST and FINAL riser x datums gives a closed modeled side-section polygon, but these artificial vertical end-closing edges are NOT top/bottom bearing cuts. Minimum modeled perpendicular throat = D − riser height/sqrt(1+m²), and modeled section face area = horizontal flight run × (D*sqrt(1+m²) − riser height/2). Optional measured lower and upper horizontal support surface references lie outside the nominal notch span and do not create or certify bearing cuts.
tools.example: 105 in between finished floors, 14 risers and 10 in tread run yield 7.5 in risers, 13 treads, 130 in horizontal run, 162.5 in first-tread-to-landing notch pitch reference and about 167.1 in floor-to-floor diagonal (not a board cut length). With 1.5 in tread stock and no later lower finish, bottom trim reference is 6 in. A separately entered 1.25 in tread-nose projection starts the first nose at x=−1.25 in; a 36 in upper landing reference extends from x=130 to x=166 in without changing the 130 in nominal stringer notch run. With 7.5 in rise/step, 10 in tread and 11.25 in stock normal depth, the lower parallel reference edge is y=0.75x−6.5625 in; the modeled minimum throat is 5.25 in, and the 130 in long nominal cross-sectional envelope has 1340.625 in² face area (a geometry reference, NOT lumber purchase area). Optional 3 in lower and 6 in upper horizontal support surface runs are separately indicated, not transferred automatically to saw cuts.
tools.limit: Nominal straight-stair *reference* only. The floor-to-floor diagonal is NOT a stringer cut length or stock length.
